vignette:
He is seventy-eight now, a soft-spoken African man who has spent most of his working life as a librarian, moving carefully among shelves, repairing worn bindings, and guiding students toward the books they do not yet know they need. He has been married for more than fifty years. When he speaks about his life before the bombing, he does so with the steadiness of someone describing a well-ordered room: work in the library during the day, tea with his wife in the evening, prayers, neighborhood conversations, grandchildren climbing into his lap with schoolbooks and questions. He had lived through political unrest before, but he carried himself as if routine and learning could still make the world understandable.

The attack happens on an ordinary morning. He is in the public reading room, sorting returned newspapers and listening to the low rustle of pages turning. A young man leaves a bag near the entrance. He notices it only vaguely, the way librarians notice objects left where they should not be. He thinks he will ask about it after he finishes stacking the papers. Then the explosion tears through the room. He remembers light first, then a sound so large it seems to erase all other sounds. Glass bursts inward. Shelves collapse. The air fills with dust, heat, and the smell of burning paper. For several seconds he does not understand that he is on the floor. His ears ring. Someone is screaming for God. Someone else is screaming for a child.

He crawls because he cannot stand. His hands slide over wetness he realizes is blood, though he does not know whose. He sees a student he recognizes lying motionless beside an overturned chair. He tries to lift part of a shelf pinning another man's leg, but his arms shake and fail him. Outside, sirens and shouting merge into one long metallic roar. Later he learns that several people have died, including two regular library visitors whose reading habits he knew by heart. He survives with cuts, bruising, and a shoulder injury. For weeks, neighbors call him fortunate.

At first he tells the story the way survivors often do, in facts. There was an explosion. Many people were hurt. The library is damaged. But in his body, nothing returns to normal. He startles violently at dropped books, slamming doors, motorcycles backfiring in the street. If a plastic bag is left unattended in a market or bus station, his chest tightens and his mouth goes dry. His wife notices that he no longer sits with his back to a doorway. In restaurants and waiting rooms, he scans every face, every entrance, every object on the floor. He says he is "being careful," but the vigilance exhausts him.

Sleep becomes the worst part of the day. He dreads bedtime because the dreams come as soon as he closes his eyes: dust in his throat, burning paper, a hand reaching from under debris. Sometimes in the dream he hears no explosion at all, only the terrible silence just before it. He wakes gasping, disoriented, gripping the mattress as if it were the library floor. His wife reaches for him and he flinches before he recognizes her. On some nights he gets up and walks through the house checking windows and locks, then sits in the dark until dawn.

Returning to work feels both necessary and unbearable. The rebuilt library is cleaner, brighter, safer by all official measures, yet he experiences it as haunted. The smell of old books, once comforting, now can suddenly carry him back to smoke and scorched paper. When students drop backpacks beside tables, he cannot concentrate until he knows who they belong to. If someone lingers near the entrance or leaves abruptly, his mind races ahead into catastrophe. He has begun asking younger staff to handle crowded events because the press of bodies and noise makes him feel trapped. He hates this change in himself. Librarianship has always required patience and openness; now he finds himself watching people with suspicion.

He also carries a quieter burden he rarely names directly. He thinks of the student on the floor, of the man whose leg he could not free, and of how he himself crawled toward the exit. He knows, rationally, that he was injured and dazed, that no elderly man could have done more in that chaos. Still, the thought returns when he is shelving books or pouring tea: I left them there. On anniversaries of the attack and whenever there is news of another bombing, he grows withdrawn. He avoids television, then seeks it out compulsively, as if watching might help him master what happened. It never does.

His world has become smaller over the years. He still goes to the library, still dresses carefully, still exchanges polite greetings with neighbors. To outsiders he appears dignified, even serene. But his wife knows how often he refuses weddings, markets, buses, and public celebrations. His grandchildren know he loves them, but they also know not to jump on him from behind. He says he misses the man he was before that morning, the man who could enter a room and think first about books rather than exits. Even now, in safety, some part of him remains on that library floor, listening for the next blast.
